conceptTag: Why great technology waits for complements
readerTitle: The barcode worked in 1974. Why did stores wait?
caseNote: 실제 사례 (1974년 UPC 바코드 첫 스캔과 느린 확산) + 가상 적용 (식품 유통업체, 미용실 예약 앱)
insight: 기술의 가치는 기술 자체가 아니라 그 기술을 쓸모 있게 만드는 보완재가 얼마나 갖춰졌는지에 달려 있다.
misconception: 기술이 충분히 뛰어나면 고객은 알아서 쓴다. 안 쓰는 건 기술이 부족하거나 홍보가 부족해서다.

sources.text: Brown, S. A. (1997). Revolution at the Checkout Counter: The Explosion of the Bar Code. Harvard University Press.
GS1 US, history of the UPC barcode (first scan, Marsh Supermarket, Troy, Ohio, 26 June 1974)
Adner, R. (2012). The Wide Lens: What Successful Innovators See That Others Miss. (보완재와 생태계 위험)
Shapiro, C. & Varian, H. (1999). Information Rules. Harvard Business School Press. (보완재 개념)

factChecks.note: 첫 UPC 스캔: 1974년 6월 26일 미국 오하이오주 트로이의 Marsh 슈퍼마켓, Wrigley 껌 한 팩. GS1 US 자료로 날짜와 장소를 다시 확인하세요.
1970년대 후반까지 스캐너 도입이 느렸다는 내용은 Brown(1997)에 근거합니다. 정확한 매장 수·비율은 자료마다 달라 카드에는 수치를 쓰지 않고 "for years, few stores"로만 적었습니다.
1973년 미국 식료품 업계 위원회가 공통 코드 표준(UPC)을 선정했다는 내용을 Brown(1997) 또는 GS1 자료로 확인하세요. 카드 6에 "in 1973"으로 적었습니다.
유통업체·미용실 사례의 수치(태그 부착 15%, 종이 예약장 60%)는 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: The barcode worked in 1974. Why did stores wait?
body: In June 1974, a cashier at a supermarket in Troy, Ohio, scanned a pack of chewing gum. The beep worked. The price appeared. Checkout was faster and more accurate.
Yet for years afterward, few stores bought scanners. The technology wasn't the problem.

image.label: A pack of gum passing over an early checkout scanner
image.brief: 1970년대 슈퍼마켓 계산대. 껌 한 팩이 빨간 레이저 스캐너 위를 지나가는 장면, 따뜻한 레트로 색감. 실제 브랜드 로고나 포장 디자인은 쓰지 않음. 배경 진열대의 상품들에는 바코드가 거의 없도록 표현.

cards.title: A faster scanner, but few tagged products.
body: You run a food distributor with four warehouses. A vendor offers handheld readers for a new tag that tracks pallets automatically. In a demo, receiving is three times faster.
The catch: only about 15% of your suppliers put the tag on their pallets. What do you do?

options.text: Buy readers for all four warehouses now
options.feedback: You get the readers early, but 85% of pallets still need manual checks. You pay for speed you can't use yet.

options.text: Wait until most suppliers tag their pallets
options.feedback: Safe on cost. But suppliers may be waiting for buyers like you, so the day may never come on its own.

options.text: Pilot in one warehouse and help your biggest suppliers start tagging
options.feedback: You spend a little to create the missing piece where it matters most. The readers become useful because the tags now exist.

cards.title: Each side waited for the other.
body: A store scanner was only useful if most products carried a barcode. Food makers saw little reason to print codes until many stores could read them.
So stores waited for codes, and makers waited for scanners. Early adopters still had cashiers typing in prices for every unmarked item.
The scanner was ready in 1974. The things around it were not.

image.label: Two people each waiting at opposite ends of a bridge
image.brief: 다리 양쪽 끝에 각각 서 있는 두 인물. 왼쪽은 계산대 스캐너를 든 가게 주인, 오른쪽은 상품 상자를 든 제조업체 직원. 서로 상대가 먼저 건너오길 기다리는 표정. 다리 가운데는 비어 있음. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Complements
body: **Complements** are the other products, services or habits that must exist for a technology to deliver its value. A scanner needs barcodes. A car needs roads and fuel. A phone needs apps.
A useful way to think: the value customers get is the technology *multiplied by* its complements. If the complements are close to zero, the result is close to zero, however good the technology is.

cards.title: Look for what else has to be true.
body: Before customers can benefit, a chain of things usually has to be in place:
list: **Partners:** suppliers, retailers or installers who must adopt too
**Standards:** a shared format so pieces fit together
**Skills:** staff or customers who know how to use it
cards.callout: If one link is missing, the whole chain delivers little.
cards.softwareNote: For software, complements are often integrations and data. A brilliant tool that can't connect to the systems customers already use, or that needs data they don't collect, sits unused.

cards.title: Someone has to supply the missing piece.
body: The grocery industry helped itself. In 1973, an industry committee agreed on one shared code format, so a maker printed one code that every scanner could read.
That didn't fix adoption overnight, but it removed one reason to wait. Over time, as more products carried codes, each new scanner became more valuable, and more stores bought them.
The lesson: winners often build, fund or organize the complement instead of waiting for it.

image.label: A chain of linked pieces with one gap being filled
image.brief: 사슬 고리 인포그래픽. 고리마다 "Scanner", "Shared code", "Printed barcodes", "Trained cashiers" 라벨. 한 고리가 비어 있고 손이 그 자리에 새 고리를 끼워 넣는 모습.

cards.title: Supplying complements is costly and risky.
body: Building the missing piece yourself can cost more than the technology. And some complements never arrive, no matter how long you wait.
There's a second trap: whoever controls a scarce complement may capture much of the value. If you depend on one partner's piece, they can raise the price later.
So map the complements early, decide which you'll provide, and which you can afford to depend on.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app for salons.
body: Your app fills a hair salon's last-minute empty slots by alerting nearby customers. Salon owners love the demo.
But about 60% of the salons you target still keep appointments in a paper book, so the app can't see their open slots. What's your best move?

options.text: Spend more on ads so more salons hear about the app
options.feedback: You'd reach more owners, but most still couldn't use it. More awareness doesn't fix a missing piece.

options.text: Include a simple free digital calendar and help salons move their bookings in
options.feedback: It costs you building and onboarding time, but you create the complement your app needs, and the calendar keeps salons with you.

options.text: Sell only to the 40% already using digital calendars
options.feedback: Fast and cheap to start, but it caps your market, and you depend on whichever calendar tools those salons use.

cards.title: Great technology is only as valuable as what surrounds it.
body: When customers don't adopt something that clearly works, look for the missing complement before blaming the product.
**Try it today:** pick one tool or offer you're pushing. List three things a customer needs besides it to get the benefit. Which one is missing, and who could supply it?
